source.title: A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment
source.authors: Amanda Askell; Yuntao Bai; Anna Chen; Dawn Drain; Deep Ganguli; T. Henighan; Andy Jones; Nicholas Joseph; B. Mann; Nova DasSarma; Nelson Elhage; Zac Hatfield-Dodds; Danny Hernandez; John Kernion; Kamal Ndousse; Catherine Olsson; D. Amodei; Tom B. Brown; Jack Clark; Sam McCandlish; Chris Olah; J. Kaplan

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the original scaling-law work and fixes its model aspect ratio based on a cited finding about what is roughly optimal. Its own scaling experiments concern preference modeling and alignment evaluations, not the claim’s held-out language-model pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model-size trends for preference-model losses and downstream preference-model evaluations (Figures 27–28), but these are not measurements of held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy, token/compute scaling, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. It fixes aspect ratio rather than varying architecture details. No claim-version rows are warranted; the related preference-model results are recorded as none-version findings.
record.test_reason: The study's own Figures 27 and 28 plot held-out preference-model loss against model size (13M–52B) for preference-model pre-training and fine-tuning. The authors label Figure 27 "Scaling laws for PMP" and comment on whether the curves follow a power law. V5 explicitly covers fine-tuning and transfer regimes, so these results bear on V5 in a new setting. They are a side result, and the values are figure-only.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The authors also conclude that simple HHH prompting improves alignment evaluations with scale at little alignment tax on large models, and that context distillation approximates prompting. They find ranked preference modeling beats and outscales imitation learning, while binary discrimination does not. PMP, best with binarized data, improves sample efficiency. On scaling laws they only observe that PM losses follow rough, sometimes deviating, power-law trends, with an unexplained off-trend 52B.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies preference-model and imitation-learning objectives, preference-model pre-training, and downstream alignment evaluations; it does not reproduce the original language-model pretraining loss or compute-allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that preference-model loss scaling can deviate from a clean power-law trend, including an off-trend 52B result in Figure 27; it does not identify this as sensitivity in the original claim’s exponents or compute-optimal split.
record.problems: For the scaling results relevant to the claim’s subject, values are presented in figures without tabulated numbers or reported uncertainty. The models use a fixed architecture aspect ratio, and the paper does not vary training tokens or compute to assess the original claim.

untested.parts: Language-model pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute; the LM pretraining runs are described but their loss curves are not reported.
Extrapolation from small to large runs.
Compute-optimal allocation; all models are trained for a fixed 400B tokens.
Shape is fixed at d_model = 128 n_layer, citing Kaplan et al.
Other modalities, repeated data, and token or compute scaling in the fine-tuning regime; only parameter scaling is shown.
The paper does not frame downstream accuracy-vs-size curves as predictability, nor relate them to pretraining loss.
Fit or setup dependence of exponents; no fits are reported.

missing.what: Human-preference Elo is linear in log model size from 197M to 13B, then flat from 13B to 52B; authors attribute the plateau to evaluator limits. This is related to downstream scaling but is not framed as predictability.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's gate placed the study at T4/uses_without_test. I reclassify it as a T3 test of V5 only, because Figures 27 and 28 directly report loss-vs-parameter scaling in fine-tuning and transfer regimes and comment on power-law form. The evidence is weak: figure-only values, no fitted exponents, and parameters are the only scaled axis. The aspect ratio is fixed by citing Kaplan et al., which is a use of V4, not a test.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, and compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as compute varies.
Comparisons of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds across modalities or other training regimes.
Prediction of downstream performance from language-model pretraining loss or scale.
Dependence of the original laws’ fitted exponents or compute-optimal split on setup and fitting choices.

conditions.value: Learn to Summarize, HellaSwag, and Ethics evaluations

rows.value: figure only; the authors state that larger models perform better, with sometimes fairly clean power-law trends and often significant deviations
rows.note: The stated trends concern preference-model comparison loss after fine-tuning, not language-model pretraining cross-entropy.
rows.check: Best-achieved fine-tuning comparison loss falls with size. The authors say it is sometimes fairly clean power-law and often shows significant deviations, including a slope change near 100M parameters. The record says 'or no pre-training', but Figure 28 is titled 'Finetuning Performance After PMP'.

relationships.condition: Preference-model pre-training on StackExchange, Reddit, Wikipedia and Mix; held-out PM loss vs size, 13M–52B
relationships.reason: Loss falls with size roughly along a trend, but the 52B model is off-trend and the authors cannot explain it (r1–r3; figure-only).
relationships.display_finding: Loss generally decreased with model size, but the 52B model departed from the trend for unexplained reasons.

relationships.condition: Preference-model fine-tuning after PMP on Learn to Summarize, HellaSwag and Ethics; best test loss vs size
relationships.reason: Larger models are always better, but the authors report the power law is only sometimes clean, with significant deviations and slope changes (r4).
relationships.display_finding: Larger models consistently performed better, although power laws were only sometimes clean and showed substantial deviations and slope changes.
